en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who was a bearer of the burden of the tradition of the illustrious teacher Prabhākara.
Adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and with critical notes (*ṭippaṇī*) on difficult passages, [this work] is named *Śāstramukha*.
First Chapter:
Declaration of the Subject Matter of the Chapter.
We shall now exert ourselves in investigating the meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*).
According to the view of Prabhākara-guru, for the sake of establishing the commencement of Mīmāṃsā. // 1 //
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) against the commencement of the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra according to the Bhaṭṭa school: Here, some maintain that the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra need not be commenced.
For it is merely a compendium of logical principles (nyāya) serving as a means for investigating the meaning of Vedic sentences.
Furthermore, there is no meaning of a Vedic sentence that is to be investigated as the object of inquiry;
nor does it stand to reason that such an object, once investigated and determined, serves a purpose [for the Vedas].
Because it would not serve a human purpose (*apuruṣārthatvāt*).
For if it were to serve a human purpose, the Vedic injunction alone would be its authority;
yet an injunction whose meaning is not intended to be conveyed cannot function as a valid means of knowledge.
Is it not the case that, because words possess an innate connection (*autpattika*) with their meanings, it is improper for them to have meanings that are not intended to be expressed?
True, this is so;
however, since the Veda itself makes known its own orientation toward something else, the resulting state of having an unintended meaning cannot be avoided.
For instance,

in the injunction "one's own Veda should be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), there is understood a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) constricted by an injunction consisting of the instigation of another, which is expressed by the suffix *tavya*. And that [activity], by its very nature, requires an object to be produced (*bhāvya*), an instrument (*karaṇa*), and a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
In this regard, first of all, study alone, as expressed by the same word, cannot be connected as the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*),
because it is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*).

For if that were accepted as the end to be accomplished, human engagement would be impossible, which would result in the collapse of the function of the injunction (*vidhi*), which consists in the impelling of another.

Nor can the connection of the *svādhyāya* (the Vedic text) being mentioned in syntactic coordination with [the injunction] as the *bhāvya* (the result to be accomplished) be conceived through a single sentence, because that would entail the futility of the injunction;
for even without an injunction, it is understood that the *svādhyāya* is indeed acquired through study.
Nor can it be said that this injunction is for the purpose of restriction— as in the case of "one threshes rice"—
because study does not have the sacrifice as its purpose;
indeed, the rules regarding study are not restricted solely to the context of the sacrifice.
It is not [contradicted] with respect to the intrinsic nature of the rice and so forth;

for since the accomplishment of the fruit of the sacrifice is achieved by means of rice-grains produced precisely through threshing, and this is not within the scope of any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its establishment by that very means involves no contradiction whatsoever.

However, the apprehension of the intrinsic nature of the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is established by the act of recitation (*adhyayana*) alone; thus, when this is restricted [to that specific means], it contradicts other means of knowledge.

For it is observed that even one who does not study himself may grasp the Veda (*svādhyāya*) being recited by another person. Furthermore, the accomplishment of the ritual fruit through the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) cannot depend solely on the Veda as accepted through formal study; since [the Veda] would thus lack a connection to the ritual by not serving the purpose of the ritual, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) would be untenable.
By this very reasoning, the connection of "comprehension of meaning" (*arthāvabodha*) as the objective to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) should also be understood as refuted.
For instance:

although it is observed that from the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya) there arises an understanding of fruitful ritual acts, and thus that [study] alone is determined to be the end to be accomplished (bhāvya), nevertheless, even without an injunction, the fact that study is a means for the comprehension of meaning is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); therefore, the injunction would indeed be purposeless.

Nor does the restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) "the comprehension of meaning must be cultivated through study alone" possess purposefulness, because since that comprehension is possible by other means as well, such a restriction is untenable.

Furthermore, a restriction cannot be established in the sense that "only those who comprehend the meaning through study and then perform [the rites] achieve the realization of the fruit of the sacrifice."

Because study does not have the ritual as its purpose, when it follows that heaven alone must be postulated as the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*) according to the *Viśvajit* principle, [the author] states: "Ātreya [holds that] the fruit [is attained] because of the specific mention. Thus, it is determined that the end to be achieved is precisely the attainment of all desired fruits—such as the satisfaction of the ancestors and the resulting favor obtained through streams of honey and ghee mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
But surely, in the initial study [of the Veda], no fruit based on an explanatory passage (arthavāda) is heard,
because such explanatory passages are not heard there;
for these are indeed explanatory passages for the injunctions regarding retention, recitation, and sacrifice.
Regarding this, the venerable authors of the Vārttika say:
"In the case of the first [type of] study, there is no mention whatsoever of a fruit;
and that [mention of a fruit] which exists for retention and for the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is likewise refuted."
Thus it is said.
This is true;
nevertheless, since those [auxiliaries] are obtained through extended application (atideśa), it is indeed logical that their fruit is to be brought about. For instance:

In sentences containing optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like, two types of productive energy (*bhāvanā*) are understood: the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) and the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*). Among these, the verbal productive energy consists in the instigation of another.
The activity of the person (puruṣapravṛtti) is what is to be brought about (bhāvya).

And the relationship between the optative suffixes (liṅādi) and that instigation (preraṇā), which consists in the denoted-denoter relation (vācyavācakabhāva), serves as the instrument (karaṇa) therein by virtue of its fitness (yogyatā).
Regarding this, the venerable authors of the Vārttika state:

"The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others both impel and express [the injunction]" (Tantravārttika 1.2.1). Furthermore, the praise found in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) constitutes the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), by virtue of its suitability for generating a desire in the person being impelled.

Thus, in the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), where no explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is directly heard, the *śabdabhāvanā*—which requires an *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance)—appropriates explanatory passages through extension (*atideśa*) from the study of the *japayajña*.

As the venerable authors of the Vārttika have said: "Others [the explanatory passages] are obtained through syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*), inference (*anumāna*), and so forth, as well as by way of extension (*atideśa*)."
And those extended *arthavādas* provide the fruit for the efficient-force (*arthabhāvanā*), as in the case of the *Rātrisatra*.

Thus, when the fruit mentioned in the *arthavāda* is determined to be the goal (*bhāvya*), the study (*adhyayana*)—which is expressed in the same word—is connected as fulfilling its requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*).

And so, by the maxim that "when [the fruit] arises from one [element], the others are for its sake," even the mass of syllables denoted by the word *svādhyāya* is determined to exist solely for the purpose of accomplishing the study.
And thus, since the syllables are directed toward something else, the comprehension of meaning from them is altogether untenable, due to the absence of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*);
for in the linguistic usage of elders, it is only syllables that are not directed elsewhere which are conventionally established as signifiers of meaning.
Furthermore, a word conveys its meaning only in dependence upon linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*).
As for the comprehension of meaning that arises even from syllables intended for something else,

that must be understood as nothing but an error, based on the mistaken impression that those syllables are not intended for anything else, due to the observation of a general correlation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Furthermore, an object that is not being perceived is neither the subject matter nor the purpose of inquiry; thus, inquiry should not be undertaken. And if it is not undertaken, even the thorough knowledge of the methods (nyāya) that serve as its means is useless.
And if that [Veda] is not useful, then the Mīmāṃsā treatise based upon it should not be commenced; such is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
The justification for the commencement of Mīmāṃsā according to the Bhaṭṭa school:

The final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is that because the injunction "one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" makes it known that the *svādhyāya* is the object (*karman*), it is understood as the very thing to be brought into being (*bhāvya*).
Although the *svādhyāya* cannot be a "productive object" (*nirvartya-karman*) due to its eternality, [it is nonetheless the goal].

Or [it may be] the status of an object as something to be modified (*vikārya-karmatā*), since no modification of it through study is possible; nevertheless, its status as an object by way of being attained (*prāpyatayā*) is not untenable.
For this very reason, the author of the Vṛtti cites the study of the Vedas as an example of an action that reaches its object;
and it is logical that the activity is directed solely toward that which is the object.
This is the scriptural application of the Vedic injunction.
Nor is it untenable for the study of the text to be a subordinate element, like the flour;
for it is useful as a means for the comprehension of the meaning which bears fruit.
Even though the utility for understanding the meaning is not apprehended prior to the study,

nevertheless, it certainly exists as a purpose even when occurring subsequently. And it is not illogical for something to have the status of a subordinate element (*śeṣitva*) by virtue of a future utility, just like the case of the sacrificial fires (*agni*).
For there is the comprehension of the application (*viniyoga*) of fires that have already arisen, not the arising of those whose application has not yet been comprehended;

because words such as *āhavanīya* have non-worldly referents, their meaning is not understood prior to the comprehension of their linguistic derivation, and thus an application in acts such as the *homa* sacrifice would be impossible.
And so it has been said:

"For a substance (dravya) deserves refinement (saṃskāra) only when it is of use in the past or the future" [Tantravārttika 2.1.4]. Now, it might be argued that the injunction for refinement is indeed purposeless, since its utility lies solely in the comprehension of meaning.
It is not meaningless,
because it possesses purpose by way of being a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). But is it not the case that a restrictive rule is impossible?

It was stated that there is no contact with the sacrifice (*kratu*); however, that is not possible, because if one follows the sense that [the Veda] has an intrinsic nature, it is only appropriate that there be contact with the sacrifice when it enters into the sacrifice.
Indeed, if the entry of the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) into the sacrifice were not accepted, [the aforementioned would be untenable].

In that case, the inherent capacity of words—whose meanings have been mastered through the linguistic usage of elders—to convey their own natural meanings would be lost. Furthermore, it is not logical for words to abandon their own primary meanings (*jahatsvārthatva*). Therefore, it is proper that the refinement (*saṃskāra*) resulting from study should indeed enter into the productive realization (*bhāvanā*) of the fruit of the sacrifice.

In this regard, the description of the restriction concerning ritual injunctions is as follows: the accomplishment of the productive realization of the sacrificial fruit occurs for those who perform the rites after understanding their meaning solely through the ritual injunctions manifested by means of Vedic study.

In the case of the *arthavādas*, however, the sacrifices being performed—encouraged by the *arthavādas* whose meanings have been manifested through study—are sufficient for the realization of the fruit.

In the case of the *mantras*, moreover, the recollection of the ritual elements (*padārtha*) during the sacrifices by means of the very *mantras* grasped through study is an auxiliary to the realization of the fruit.
Furthermore, the restriction of time and the restriction of vows and so forth are dependent upon the rule of study.
“Having performed the opening ceremony according to the rule on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin,
being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months.”

[Manu Smṛti, Chapter 2, Verses 49–51] “An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should go about begging for alms with ‘bhavat’ at the beginning; a Kṣatriya, however, with ‘bhavat’ in the middle; and a Vaiśya, with ‘bhavat’ at the end.”
[Manu Smṛti 2.2, 49, 11].
Thus, because the syllables do not have any other purpose, and because the inquiry yields the understanding of fruitful ritual action, it acquires its subject matter and purpose;

and since the inquiry follows immediately after Vedic study once the subject matter and purpose are established, the stay at the teacher’s house becomes meaningful, and one must therefore terminate that stay immediately after study.

Demonstrating that the Smṛti injunction, "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe," is based on an improper principle, and considering that the Veda's own study (svādhyāya) intends its actual meaning by virtue of its purpose being the comprehension of that meaning, the author of the Sūtras states the subject matter and the purpose of the inquiry: "Now, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā 1.1.1).
And this has been explained: "Now, therefore, this first sūtra, 'The desire to know dharma,' was composed to state the subject matter called dharma and the purpose of Mīmāṃsā."
Thus, although much has been said, it is incorrect;
for in sentences containing [optative] suffixes such as *liṅ*, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) does not require another object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*),
because the new potency (*apūrva*) as the object to be accomplished is expressed by its own word.

For it has been demonstrated with great precision in the *Viṣayakaraṇīya* that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like denote only that efficient force (*bhāvanā*) which has become subordinate to the *apūrva*, which is the primary element situated within the category of the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*).

Consequently, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is no connection with the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) to satisfy the expectancy for an end to be accomplished;
nor, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), is there a syntactic connection of the Veda itself (*svādhyāya*) as the thing to be accomplished.
How, then, is the fruit such as heaven postulated in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others? Listen to how it is so:

that *apūrva* which is understood to be the object to be accomplished (*kārya*) obtains its very existence through the performance of sacrifices and other means that serve as instruments (*karaṇa*) connected to it as their objective (*viṣaya*).
And without an agent, the performance of that [action] is not possible;
nor is the status of being an agent obtained without eligibility (adhikāra);
and eligibility is not established without one who is to be enjoined (niyojya).
Alternatively, since an unqualified person cannot be conceived as the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the desire for heaven (*svargakāmanā*) is postulated as a qualifying attribute.

If the desire for heaven is indeed a qualification of the person to be enjoined, then, like the *agnihotra* and other rites, heaven must also be accomplished through the force of the injunction (*niyoga*).
Let it be so.

"In that case, even here, let the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) be connected as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (niyojya), just as in the case of the Rātrisatra sacrifice. No;
because the performance [of the action] is established from another source.
From what other source?
Because it is prompted by the injunction for the act of becoming an *ācārya*.
But what is the injunction for the act of becoming an *ācārya*?
"That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda..."
They declare that teacher to be one who possesses both the ritual manual (kalpa) and the secret teachings (rahasya).

Based on the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Manu (2.140), it is inferred that one should bring about the status of a teacher (ācāryatva) by initiating a pupil and teaching him the Veda; and since this status of a teacher is non-worldly (alaukika), like the Āhavanīya fire and other such sacrificial fires, it is entirely appropriate to enjoin the means for its accomplishment.
In this regard, by implication, only one who desires to become a teacher has the qualification [to perform these rites], just as there is a restriction regarding the rules for acquiring wealth.

In this regard, because one observes the performance of beneficial acts and the giving of fees prescribed for the student, the desire to become a teacher belongs only to one who seeks those [rewards].

Just as the status of being initiated (*dīkṣitatva*) is established by the initiation rite (*dīkṣaṇīyā*), so too the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*) is established by the teaching of the Veda.

Furthermore, since the act of initiation (*upanayana*), as understood through the suffix *ktvā* (denoting a prior action), must have the same agent as the act of teaching (*adhyāpana*), it cannot possess this common agency without being part of a single performance (*ekaprayoga*).

And since a single performance is untenable without a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), initiation stands as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) with respect to the act of teaching, which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the realization of the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka-bhāvanā*).

And the restrictive rule, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa of eight years," is dependent upon that [initiation]. Initiation does not, by its own nature, have the purpose of bringing about the presence of the one to be initiated; rather, it is a subsidiary (aṅga) to it precisely through that [presence]. Nor is the presence of the one to be initiated—who is otherwise useless with respect to teaching—useful for teaching; therefore, when there is a requirement for an object (karman) for initiation, initiation [is performed].
Having proceeded thus, it is understood that the study enjoined by the rule "one's own Veda is to be studied" is an act for the sake of the initiated boy;
and since study is useful for the purpose of teaching,
this is consistent.

13. Therefore, the initiation (*upanayana*) of the young student (*māṇavaka*) who is about to engage in the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) is 14. an auxiliary to the act of teaching; thus, the injunction for teaching, while employing initiation as its own constituent part, also employs the study [of the Veda] because it would otherwise be impossible [to accomplish the teaching]. And the injunction for the private recitation of the Veda, having achieved its fulfillment through the completion of that study prompted by the teaching, does not require any other separate qualification (*adhikāra*).
Therefore, this is not the domain of the *viśvajit*-rule,
nor is it the domain of the *rātrisatra*-rule, because those two concern injunctions (*niyoga*) whose objects are not prompted by anything else.
For this very reason, those two [the injunctions for study and teaching] do not apply to the performance of the *prayāja* and other such subsidiary rites.

Otherwise, even according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since Vedic study would be prompted by injunctions concerning specific desires (*kāma-śruti*), Śūdras and others would possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for ritual acts accomplished through knowledge (*vidyā*).

Therefore, because study is prompted by the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*), only those who have undergone initiation (*upanayana*) obtain the mantras prompted by that [injunction]; thus, Śūdras and others lack qualification.
And thus, since the study is prompted by another injunction, a prima facie objection based on the *rātrisatra* logic is not appropriate.
Nor is it logical that the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) arises because [study] is not so prompted, while the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) arises because it is so prompted.
Because there would be no cause for its being not so employed;
and as for what was said— that an injunction is for the purpose of restriction—
that too is incorrect.

Because the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" (svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ) is meaningful through its prescription for the purpose of fulfilling a mandate (niyoga), a mandatory suffix (*tavya*) expresses an injunction. Furthermore, this cannot be construed as a mere restatement of an injunction whose object is a ritual sacrifice (*kratu*), as is the case with [injunctions such as] "one should thresh" (*avahanti*) and the like.
Because the ritual injunctions are not present;
for it is only by virtue of their presence that there is recognition of the ritual injunctions, and thus one may admit the restatement of those ritual injunctions therein.
But here, no such presence exists.
Nor is there a recognition of the ritual injunction through the mediation of a connection between word-meanings— as in the case of "The ladle made of parṇa-wood becomes a means of protection"—
because the Veda as one's own study (svādhyāya) has a relationship with rituals that is not invariable,
since we observe that meaningless elements such as "hum" and so forth are included within the svādhyāya.
Precisely because the injunction (*niyoga*) is understood here as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*),

for that very reason it is not possible for the Veda (*svādhyāya*) to be connected [to the injunction] as a desired object (*īpsita-karman*), since two things to be accomplished cannot coexist within a single sentence.

Nor can there be non-contradiction on the grounds that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is connected as a qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), as is the case with heaven and other such rewards; for the acquisition of the Veda is not a fruit produced by an injunction.
For only that which is a fruit of an injunction [can be so related].

That very [study] alone, as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and nothing else; this was demonstrated in the third [book] at the passage:
“You are ignorant of the objects and the persons to be enjoined.

Therefore, since its purposefulness is established simply by the presentation of the injunction regarding the object of study, there is no need to assume that the injunction has the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the sake of entering into Vedic sacrifices.
The view of the Elder Prabhākara and its refutation.

Others, however, formulate the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) as follows: study is prompted by the injunction to teach and is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that teaching; and because the Veda (*svādhyāya*) exists for the sake of accomplishing that [teaching], it is not intended to convey its own meaning (*avivakṣitārthatā*).
That is incorrect;
for the status of being "for that purpose" (tādarthya) does not follow from mere application alone.

It might be argued: just as in the case of the Prajāpati-vows, because an independent agent is understood, there is a postulation of a person to be enjoined (niyojya) for the sake of establishing the entitlement (adhikāra) which is the cause of that [agency].
"Likewise, because we observe its application [to that end], it must have that as its purpose"—
this is not so,
because application deviates from having that specific purpose.
Even in the absence of such a purpose (tādarthya), study is employed by the injunctions for sacrifices merely by virtue of being a source of assistance.
How then is the singularity of the animal (*paśvekatva*) and so forth an auxiliary (*aṅga*)?

It is not the case that the case-ending itself expresses singularity and so forth as related to the sacrifice, whereby there would be an application (*viniyoga*) through syntactical connection (*vākya*), as is the case with the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) and the like.
For case-endings directly denote their own meaning as residing precisely within the meaning of the nominal stem;
nor is the singularity of that which functions as an instrument expressed, nor is the status of being an instrument attributed to that which is already endowed with number.
Because instrumentality and oneness are denoted simultaneously,
the status of being a subordinate element (śeṣatva) based on syntactic application does not belong to the number expressed by the case-ending;
yet, such subordinacy is indeed required.
And that [subservience] is indeed produced by application (*prayukti*).
Not so;
for even there, the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) is not based on direct statement (*aupādānika*), but rather is inferential (*laiṅgika*) alone.

The capacity of the thing itself (*vastusāmarthya*) is what is called the inferential mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, since number by its very nature delimits the object to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), it has the object to be numbered as its sole purpose; however, because there would otherwise be a contradiction with the connection to the *grāhaka* (the agent who grasps), when there is a mere relation to the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which constitutes the object to be numbered, the relation to the animal and so forth that constitute the *grāhaka* is derived through implication (*aupādānika*).
For, by the mere fact of being mentioned in proximity, that which apprehends even the meaning of a case-ending expresses it precisely as connected to the purpose of the [principal] act;

and since this would otherwise be impossible, one must go beyond the relationship of essential form based on mere expression and determine a connection with the number to be accomplished as a means. Thus, in that case as well, the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*) is not merely based on syntactic inclusion (*aupādānika*).
Let it be, then, that by means of *liṅga* alone, study (*adhyayana*) is also enjoined for the purpose of teaching (*adhyāpana*).
This cannot be so,
because the application (*viniyoga*) by *liṅga* depends upon a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general relationship.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a general relationship for this [injunction].

Now, it might be argued that the hearing of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) brings about the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatā*) of the study, which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root.
That is not so.

Because the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is the cause for the arising of the activity of the one being instigated (*prayojya*), it would follow that the subordinate relationship is reversed.

Furthermore, the criteria of sentence (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyāna*) cannot even be suspected as being the factors that assign the study [of the Veda] to the purpose of teaching.
Moreover, there is a contradiction with the *Ṭīkā* text for those who maintain that [study] is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*).
For this reason, the Blessed One has said:
"Because it is something to be employed and because it is not a constituent part [of the cognition], doubt arises."
Therefore, it must be challenged as a prima facie argument precisely on the grounds that it is not an auxiliary (anaṅga). But how can it be challenged as not being an auxiliary?
It is said:
For every injunction culminates in a qualification for its performance;

yet it has already been stated that there is no qualification for anyone in the injunction to study, because such a qualification is not explicitly heard [in the text], and because it is impossible to assume one on the grounds of being prompted by the injunction to teach.

In this regard, it is logical that the very qualification (adhikāra) which exists in the injunction of the motivator (prayojaka-vidhi) is itself the purpose (prayojana), because it is the first to present itself.
Furthermore, even that which is not an auxiliary (anaṅga) to something nevertheless becomes its purpose, just as the oblations and so forth are the purpose of the fire-consecration (ādhāna).

But surely, since the fruit of study is the understanding of the action that occurs immediately thereafter, it is understood that the student alone has the qualification for study; therefore, it is more appropriate that the injunction regarding the Veda (*svādhyāya*) has that [understanding] as its purpose, because it is an internal factor.
No;
for that [understanding] occurs at a later time.
For when the application [of two rules] is equal, being internal (*antaraṅgatā*) is more powerful;

however, the application of these two governing rules (*adhikāra*) is not equal. This is because the governing rule of the injunction for performance (*prayogavidhi*) occurs first, whereas the governing rule based on the comprehension of meaning arises at a later time.

And when it is understood through the injunction for study that its purpose is the fulfillment of the qualification for the injunction to teach, then—because the Veda (*svādhyāya*) exists for the sake of completing the study and is thus subordinate to another [purpose]—its meaning is not intended to be expressed.

Since the meaning is not intended to be expressed, it need not be investigated. Thinking that one has achieved one's goal merely by the study of the Veda and that it is therefore proper to leave the teacher’s house immediately after study, the Smṛti declares: "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)."
Regarding this passage from the *Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* (6.1), bathing is not enjoined here for the sake of some transcendental merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Rather, it is stated that this marks the conclusion of the rule of non-bathing—"A student (*brahmacārī*) shall not bathe"—which was observed as an auxiliary to the study of the Veda; for when those rules cease, their cessation is naturally attained.

Furthermore, since the rules of residing in the teacher’s house (*gurukula-vāsa*) and so forth are equivalent to the rule of non-bathing, their cessation is likewise necessarily attained; thus, it is precisely the cessation of all the duties of a student that is declared to occur immediately after the completion of study.

Thus, since reflection is not implied by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), the Mīmāṃsā treatise—which consists of the logical reasoning that serves as its means—is not to be commenced; such is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
Now, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) according to our own view:
although the qualification for the impelling injunction (*prayojaka-vidhi*) occurs first, [the investigation of meaning follows].
Nevertheless, it is not logical to claim that its accomplishment [the production of the Veda] is the purpose.
Rather, since it results in the understanding of the visible meaning, it is more appropriate to rely upon the student's own entitlement— which arises after the study— as the purpose,
because it resides in the agent.
For it is logical that the agency over an action belongs to the very one who performs it, because that person is the internal factor;
nor is there any reason to assume that the qualification for the rite terminates here merely upon observing the injunction all at once.
Because the performance [of the rite] is accomplished solely through the instigation of another;

for in a case where the performance cannot be obtained prior [to the injunction] without assuming a completion within the scope of the qualification (*adhikāra*), there the qualification— though not understood prior to the performance— is established as the goal (*sādhya*) by virtue of entering into that [performance].

In this case, however, since the performance [of study] is obtained through the very application of the injunction for teaching—without having to postulate a completion of the qualification [for the student's own sake]—the priority [of the student's injunction] is irrelevant.
Because it is more intimate [to the act], it is proper that the qualification belongs to the student alone.
Thus, since the performance of the injunction for study is established by the application of another [injunction] alone, there is no person to be enjoined (niyojya).
However, an eligible person (adhikārī) certainly exists;
for whoever performs a particular action is the one entitled to it therein.
And since the purpose of study is the comprehension of meaning, the student is the one entitled to it.
Furthermore, this qualification is not understood prior to the study, but is understood at a time subsequent to the study.

The study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) is accomplished in this manner: "Having performed the ritual opening (*upākaraṇa*) according to rule on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada..."
A Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedic meters for four and a half months.
"From that point on, however, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic meters during the bright fortnights;
one should recite the Vedāṅgas and the secret Upaniṣads during the dark fortnights."
As stated [in the *Tantravārttika*] at Ma.

4.1.98: "In this way, when the study [of the Veda] is performed, the comprehension of the meaning arises from the Vedic sentences which have been refined by the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). And this student thinks: 'Since it makes known the rituals useful to me, my study is for my own sake.'"
This [period] of twenty-two years is the qualification for the study of the Vedas and the hearing of Mīmāṃsā;
this is the fundamental purpose of the treatise.
It is precisely with reference to this qualification that fathers and others cause some sons and other relatives to undergo initiation by means of providing wealth and other resources.
And some, being already awakened, [realize] the Self by themselves alone, because otherwise study would be impossible,
given that study is prohibited for one who has not been initiated.
“He shall not utter the Veda, except when pronouncing the *svadhā* at funeral rites;
he remains equal to a Śūdra, being blameworthy, until he is born [again] through the Vedas.”
Thus far, the presentation of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) has been made by relying on the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*), which is inferred from the Smṛti.
This is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Vivaraṇa.
Others, however, following the injunction for teaching heard directly [from scripture], say this:

if the purpose of the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) were to consist in its being subordinate to the injunction for teaching, then— since the injunction for teaching is itself included within the *svādhyāya*— the meaning [of the latter] would not be intended as significant, and thus it would be impossible for the former to be prompted by the latter.

For one's own Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā*) is indeed denoted by the term "one's own study" (*svādhyāya*). Since the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*) must necessarily be included within one's own branch for those who have directly studied it, the injunction for study (*svādhyāya*) cannot be established as having a prompting force (*prayojaka*) because its meaning is not intended to be literal; consequently, the qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs only to the student, by virtue of its utility for the subsequent comprehension of the meaning.
[This is] the purpose of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*).

[Objection: But since it is understood that the injunction "one's own Veda is to be studied" is accomplished [by the mere act of recitation], and since study exists for the sake of fulfilling that injunction, the text is directed toward something else; therefore, the intention to convey the meaning is indeed difficult to maintain.
[Reply: Not so.
If the study of the Veda had as its sole purpose the fulfillment of the injunction (*niyoga*), this might indeed be so;
however, since the comprehension of meaning (*arthāvabodha*) is also accepted as a purpose, there is also a focus on the meaning, and thus the meaning is not unintended (*avivakṣita*).
But how can there be two purposes in a single sentence?
It is said:
the accomplishment of the injunction itself is the verbal purpose.

There is no contradiction, for the purpose is indeed the comprehension of the meaning; and since that purpose called the comprehension of the meaning cannot be accomplished by mere recitation alone, the injunction for study itself implies inquiry (*vicāra*) in order to achieve its own purpose. Furthermore, because inquiry is based on reasoning (*nyāya*), and because reasonings are to be understood through the knowledge of Mīmāṃsā, and because the knowledge of Mīmāṃsā is dependent upon a teacher...

Thinking that one should return from the teacher’s house immediately after the study of the Veda, the venerable author of the Sūtras, in order to demonstrate that the Smṛti is rooted in the position of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), has said the following while prohibiting the return from the teacher’s house— which would otherwise follow immediately after Vedic study— by means of the instruction to "investigate dharma" (dharmajijñāsā):

Regarding the statement, “Now, therefore, [begins] the inquiry into Dharma,” it is only the mere withdrawal from the teacher’s household— which is opposed to the investigation of the meaning of Vedic sentences— that is prohibited,
not the cessation of all other duties such as wandering for alms, celibacy, and so forth.

Furthermore, one who has not completed the entire set of rules for the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) is not a *snātaka*; consequently, he is not entitled to take a wife, because the tradition records that it is the *snātaka* who takes a wife, as stated in the *Gautama-Dharma-Sūtra* (4.1): "A *snātaka* shall take a wife of equal status. Therefore, having remained in the teacher’s household and set aside all other duties of the student of sacred knowledge, the meaning of the Veda must be investigated.
Because that which has not been investigated cannot be determined;
if one were to return from the teacher’s house with the meaning of the Vedas undetermined, then,
having taken a wife, he would be unable to perform the obligatory and occasional duties such as the Śrauta Agnihotra due to the onset of entitlement to those rites, and would thus incur sin.

Therefore, it is established that immediately after Vedic study, the meaning of the Vedas must be investigated; thus, the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra, which is the formulation of the logic (nyāya) serving as the means for such investigation, must be commenced.
This very clear treatise (prakaraṇa), named Śāstramukha, has been composed by Śālikanātha in order to reveal the profound intent of his teacher. (2)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Treatise," in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra.
